column1: What are the three units inside a TPU TensorCore, and what is the data path from HBM to compute?
column2:
MXU — matrix multiply (systolic array), the bulk of the FLOPs.
VPU — elementwise ops (ReLU, add, mul) and reductions.
VMEM — on-chip scratchpad in the TensorCore; like L1/L2 but much larger (~128 MiB on v5e) and programmer-controlled, not a cache.

Path: HBM → VMEM → VREGs → MXU/VPU → VMEM → HBM. Nothing computes directly out of HBM. All of it is pipelined: the copies are overlapped with MXU work so the array never stalls waiting on memory.

column1: What is the native op of one MXU, and why does that force padding to 128?
column2:
One bf16[8,128] @ bf16[128,128] → f32[8,128] every 8 cycles, on a 128×128 systolic array (256×256 on v6e/Trillium).

The array's side length is fixed, so any matrix axis smaller than 128 is padded to 128 (256 on v6e) — the FLOPs spent on the padding are wasted. With 2–4 MXUs per core, tiling dims want to exceed 128 × #MXUs.

Scale: ~5e13 bf16 FLOPs/s per MXU at 1.5 GHz → ~2e14 per v5e chip. int8 runs ~2x faster, int4 ~4x.

column1: Sketch the dataflow through a 128x128 systolic array. Where does the pipeline bubble come from?
column2:
2D grid of 16,384 ALUs, each doing one multiply-add.
• Weights (RHS, 128x128) are pushed down from the top.
• Activations (LHS, 8x128) stream in from the left.
• Each cell multiplies its overlapped pair, adds the partial sum arriving from above, and passes the result down.

Bubble: both operands are loaded diagonally, so the array takes a fill period before it's saturated. After the fill, new LHS/RHS can stream in back-to-back with no additional bubble — which is why large matrices amortize it and small ones don't.

column1: VMEM vs HBM bandwidth: what's the ratio, and what does it do to the roofline?
column2:
VMEM→MXU bandwidth is roughly 22x HBM bandwidth.

So the critical arithmetic intensity for peak FLOPs drops from ~240 to ~10–20. Worked example (int8[16384,4096] weights, v5e): FLOPs-bound at B > 267 out of HBM, but B > 11 out of VMEM (~20 realistically, since you can't spend all VMEM bandwidth on weights).

Consequence: VMEM prefetch — e.g. load the FFW weights during attention to hide the load. Limit: VMEM is tiny, so a layer's weights must be small or sharded enough to fit with room to spare.

column1: Name the four communication tiers on a TPU, fastest to slowest, with per-chip v5p numbers.
column2:
1. HBM ↔ TensorCore: 2.8e12 B/s
2. ICI (chip ↔ nearest neighbors): 9e10 B/s per axis one-way, 3 axes on v5p
3. PCIe (host ↔ its tray of chips): 1.6e10 B/s — ~100x slower than HBM
4. DCN (host ↔ host): 6.25e9 B/s

Design rule: keep the bytes crossing each channel proportional to that channel's speed. Note a TPU→TPU transfer over DCN costs PCIe → NIC egress → NIC ingress → PCIe.

column1: ICI topology: which generations get which torus, and when do you actually get wraparound links?
column2:
2D torus, 4 neighbors: v2, v3, v5e, v6e. Pod caps at 16x16; beyond that, pods talk over DCN.
3D torus, 6 neighbors: v4, v5p. Superpods 16x16x16 (v4) and 16x20x28 (v5p), built from reconfigurable 4x4x4 cubes joined by optical links.

Wraparounds: only on full-cube multiples (4x4x4, 4x4x8 — not 2x2x4, since the optical switches only exist on a full cube), or on a v5e/v6e axis of exactly 16 (so 8x16 wraps the long axis). No wraparound roughly doubles comms time.

Links are nearest-neighbor only and bypass the hosts — distant chips must hop through the chips in between (vs. GPUs' switch hierarchy).

column1: Worked: 200B params in bf16 across 32 TPU v4p. Lower bound on per-step sampling latency?
column2:
2 bytes × 200e9 = 400e9 bytes total → 12.5e9 bytes/chip → ÷ 1.23e12 B/s HBM BW ≈ 10 ms.

Why it's a bound: every decode step must re-read all parameters from HBM into the MXU, so no step can beat the weight-load time. At small batch this is close to achievable — decode is HBM-bandwidth-bound, not FLOPs-bound.

column1: VPU: what's its shape and throughput relative to the MXU, and which reductions are cheap?
column2:
Shape (8 sublanes, 128 lanes), with 4 independent ALUs per position, most ops 1/cycle.
→ 8 × 128 × 4 × 1.75e9 ≈ 7e12 FLOPs/s on v5p, about 30x less than the ~2e14 MXU FLOPs/s per core. VPU work is fp32.

Reductions: along the sublane axis (8) is cheap — intra-lane shuffle by 4/2/1 plus 3 pairwise adds. Cross-lane reductions need the separate XLU, which is slow and expensive.

Control: a single scalar core fetches/dispatches everything and can issue only one DMA request per cycle — very skewed control-per-compute, which is efficient but blocks data-dependent vectorization.
